{{DISPLAYTITLE:Official, independent and hosted checkers}}
{{Plebeian|Lean theorem prover/Explainers/The small trusted core|Lean theorem prover/Explainers/Checking a proof again later}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

Someone who wants a Lean proof checked has three kinds of program to choose from. There is
the Lean kernel as the Lean project distributes it. There are checkers written independently,
which read an exported proof and check it again. And there are services that run Lean on
another party's computer. This page says where each comes from, how a project fixes which one
it uses, and what each asks the reader to trust. It ends with the arrangement Principia
Machina uses. It describes Lean 4.35.0, of 12 October 2026.

== The official toolchain ==

Lean is an open-source project, begun by Leonardo de Moura at Microsoft Research in
2013.<ref name="about">"About", lean-lang.org. [https://lean-lang.org/about lean-lang.org/about]</ref>
Since August 2023 its development has been led by the Lean FRO, a non-profit organisation
formed for that purpose.<ref name="fro">"Lean FRO", lean-lang.org. [https://lean-lang.org/lean-fro lean-lang.org/lean-fro]</ref>
The Lean kernel is not a separate download. It is the small type checker, written in C++,
inside the program <code>lean</code>, and every toolchain carries it (see
[[Lean theorem prover/System/The Lean kernel|the Lean kernel]]).

Toolchains are installed by '''elan''', the toolchain manager. Unless told otherwise, elan
fetches them from the official project repository, which it names
<code>leanprover/lean4</code>.<ref name="elan422">"Managing Toolchains with Elan", a section of ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.22.0). [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.22.0/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/Managing-Toolchains-with-Elan/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.22.0/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/Managing-Toolchains-with-Elan/]</ref>
A project fixes its version of Lean in a one-line file, <code>lean-toolchain</code>, kept with
the project's sources so that everyone who works on it uses the same
version.<ref name="elan428">"Managing Toolchains with Elan", a section of ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.28.0). [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.28.0/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/Managing-Toolchains-with-Elan/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.28.0/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/Managing-Toolchains-with-Elan/]</ref>
The reference manual advises naming an exact version there rather than a channel such as
<code>stable</code>.<ref name="elan426">"Managing Toolchains with Elan", a section of ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.26.0). [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/Managing-Toolchains-with-Elan/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.26.0/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/Managing-Toolchains-with-Elan/]</ref>
A project pinned to the version this page describes has a file reading:

<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">leanprover/lean4:v4.35.0</pre>

The page on [[Lean theorem prover/System/Lake and Lean projects|Lake and Lean projects]] shows
the file at work.

A copy of Lean compiled from its sources can be registered with elan under a name of its own,
with <code>elan toolchain link</code>; the manual describes this for work on the Lean compiler
itself.<ref name="elan430">"Managing Toolchains with Elan", a section of ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.30.0). [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.30.0/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/Managing-Toolchains-with-Elan/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.30.0/Build-Tools-and-Distribution/Managing-Toolchains-with-Elan/]</ref>
For checking proofs there is little to gain from it. A pin is useful because every reader's
copy of the Lean kernel is the same as everyone else's. A privately compiled copy is one
more thing a reader would have to trust or rule out.

== Independent checkers in the toolchain ==

Until Lean 4.35.0, checking a Lean development with a second checker meant installing and
configuring separate tools.<ref name="rn435b">"Lean 4.35.0 (2026-10-12)", in "Release Notes", ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.36.0-rc1), section "Checking Projects with lake check and lake comparator". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.36.0-rc1/releases/v4.35.0/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.36.0-rc1/releases/v4.35.0/]</ref> That version changed this. Its toolchain
includes four checkers written apart from the Lean kernel, '''lean4lean''', '''nanoda''',
'''con-leche''' and '''con-ron''', and a fifth program, <code>leanchecker-paranoid</code>, which
is the usual replay through the Lean kernel compiled with a hardened memory
allocator.<ref name="rn435">"Lean 4.35.0 (2026-10-12)", in "Release Notes", ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.35.0). [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.35.0/releases/v4.35.0/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.35.0/releases/v4.35.0/]</ref>

The same version added a Lake command, <code>lake check</code>. It compiles a project's
default targets, exports them, replays the export through the Lean kernel, and fails if
anything rests on an axiom other than the standard three. With <code>--paranoid</code> it also
runs every bundled checker and accepts the project only if all of them
do.<ref name="rn435b" />
An export made somewhere else can be checked directly: the notes give the examples of an
export made in a virtual machine and one made by someone with more computing power, and
<code>leanchecker</code> itself gained a matching option,
<code>--from-export</code>.<ref name="rn435b" /> The heavy work of compiling can therefore
happen on one computer and the check on another.

"Independent" covers a range. nanoda is written in Rust, separately from
Lean.<ref name="arena-nanoda">"nanoda", checker page, Lean Kernel Arena. [https://arena.lean-lang.org/checker/nanoda/ arena.lean-lang.org/checker/nanoda/]</ref>
lean4lean is written in Lean;<ref name="l4l">Mario Carneiro, "Lean4Lean: Verifying a Typechecker for Lean, in Lean", in ''31st International Conference on Types for Proofs and Programs (TYPES 2025)'', Leibniz International Proceedings in Informatics 384, Schloss Dagstuhl, 2026, 2:1–2:23. doi:[https://doi.org/10.4230/LIPIcs.TYPES.2025.2 10.4230/LIPIcs.TYPES.2025.2]; full version [https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14064 arXiv:2403.14064].</ref> its description in the Lean Kernel Arena notes that it
follows the C++ implementation closely and so is likely to share some of its
faults.<ref name="arena-l4l">"lean4lean", checker page, Lean Kernel Arena. [https://arena.lean-lang.org/checker/lean4lean arena.lean-lang.org/checker/lean4lean]</ref>
Recent history shows why the difference matters and also where it stops. Lean 4.33.0 fixed
soundness faults in the Lean kernel, some of which survive in an exported proof and would
mislead a check by the Lean kernel alone, unless a checker such as nanoda is run as
well.<ref name="rn433">"Lean 4.33.0", in "Release Notes", ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.35.0-rc3), section "Kernel soundness fixes and further improvements". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.35.0-rc3/releases/v4.33.0/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.35.0-rc3/releases/v4.33.0/]</ref>
Lean 4.34.0 fixed a fault that a false proof exploited, and the notes record that nanoda
accepted the same false proof.<ref name="rn434">"Lean 4.34.0", in "Release Notes", ''The Lean Language Reference'' (edition covering Lean 4.35.0-rc3), section "Kernel Soundness and Hardening". [https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.35.0-rc3/releases/v4.34.0/ lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.35.0-rc3/releases/v4.34.0/]</ref>
A second checker does not make a fault impossible. It makes a fault matter only if every
checker that runs shares it, which is why the checkers are run together and a single
refusal decides.

How exports are written and how such checkers work is the subject of
[[Lean theorem prover/System/Proof export and independent checkers|Proof export and
independent checkers]].

== Hosted services ==

Two services on the web come up in this context. Neither is a place to send a proof for a
verdict.

'''The Lean playground''' at <code>live.lean-lang.org</code> is the official web editor for
Lean.<ref name="web-lc">"lean4web", the Lean 4 web editor's source repository, leanprover-community on GitHub. [https://github.com/leanprover-community/lean4web github.com/leanprover-community/lean4web]</ref>
Lean runs on the playground's server, not in the reader's
browser.<ref name="web-hhu">"lean4web", the development copy of the Lean 4 web editor's source, hhu-adam on GitHub. [https://github.com/hhu-adam/lean4web github.com/hhu-adam/lean4web]</ref>
It is a way to try Lean without installing it. What it shows is the result of a check on a
computer the reader does not control, and it leaves nothing a third party can check later.

'''The Lean Kernel Arena''' runs many checkers on the same exported tests, some that a
correct checker must accept and some that it must reject, and publishes how each
did.<ref name="arena">Lean Kernel Arena: "presents, tests and benchmarks proof checkers for the Lean Theorem Prover". [https://arena.lean-lang.org arena.lean-lang.org]</ref>
It grades checkers, not proofs. Its results are a reasonable basis for choosing which
checkers to run and which version of each to rely on.

A service that accepted a proof and returned a verdict would add its operator, its computer
and the connection to the list of things a reader must trust. The option
<code>--from-export</code> goes the other way: the expensive work may happen anywhere, and the
check happens on a computer the person relying on it chooses.

== Principia Machina ==

[[Lean theorem prover/Applications/Principia Machina|Principia Machina]], the framework on
this wiki for testing physical hypotheses, is written in Lean and uses the official toolchain
at a pinned version. Its account of the move to Lean sets out why the Lean kernel is not
left as the only check: a fault in the Lean kernel is the one fault no proof written in Lean
can catch. The design therefore doubles it with nanoda, which reads the same definitions and
proofs from an export file and checks them again, so a wrong proof has to deceive two checkers
of different authorship. Every checker that runs must accept; one refusal is a refusal, and a
crash counts as a refusal. Each run also includes exports broken on purpose, which every
checker must refuse.<ref name="lt">"Principia Machina: the move to Lean", the page [[Principia Machina/Lean transition]] on this wiki, status as of 14 October 2026.</ref>
The broken exports test the checkers rather than the proofs: a checker set up wrongly, or one
that accepts everything, passes every good proof and fails only this test.

The wiki's own server has no Lean toolchain, so it cannot call the Lean kernel. A derivation
submitted there as a Lean proof is checked only once a small independent checker has been
shown to run within the server's limits; the server's test ran nanoda within
them.<ref name="lt" /> Until then such a proof is recorded as prose, never as
checked.<ref name="lt" />
